newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Sumitomo Asia copper empire in tatters one year on.
newsitem.headline: Sumitomo Asia copper empire in tatters one year on.

text.p: One year after revelations of the copper trading debacle that cost Japanese metal giant Sumitomo Corp $2.6 billion, its once mighty Asian copper empire is in shreds, industry sources said on Friday.

In copper markets from Thailand to Taiwan, where rogue trader Yasuo Hamanaka once ruled supreme by using profits from metal futures trading to subsidise low-priced physical sales and edge out its rivals, Sumitomo has retreated to lick its wounds.

The 500,000 tonnes a year Taiwan copper market, previously the jewel in the crown of Sumitomo's Asian business, has largely been lost to Japanese rival Marubeni Corp , as its prices became less competitive.
"Sumitomo is still a highly reputable company in Taiwan but its copper prices are not making it here," a buyer at Taiwan's Pacific Electric Wire and Cable Group told Reuters.
"Pacific's copper purchasing from Sumitomo accounts for less than half of what was before."
Sumitomo's Taiwan office declined to comment but other buyers also said Sumitomo was losing market share.
"Our procurement from Sumitomo dropped about 75 percent this year, because of price considerations," said a buyer at Huaeng Wire and Cable Corp .
Before the scandal, Sumitomo had been the pre-eminent supplier to Taiwan's copper market, competing chiefly with Marubeni, Mitsubishi Materials Corp and Mitsui Co Ltd, Taiwan buyers said.
Traders said Marubeni was likely to replace Sumitomo in 1997 as the top copper supplier for Taiwan.
Metal industry sources estimated Marubeni would grab about 16 percent of Taiwan's copper imports.
Sumitomo's competitiveness was hindered in part by its own sourcing problems, traders said.
"There is talk that some Chilean copper producers reduced supplies to Sumitomo after the scandal," a Marubeni trader said.
In Tokyo, a Sumitomo spokesman said its copper sales in the 1996/97 fiscal year ending in March plunged by 65 percent from a year earlier to 291.9 billion yen ($2.56 billion).
"After the scandal, we suspended copper dealing. It has no relation to the physical business," he said, declining to elaborate.
"Sumitomo's offer prices are rising gradually. They're still competitive, but I'm not sure if they can maintain their share in Japan," said a senior official at a major brass maker.

Sumitomo formerly had an estimated 40 percent share of Thailand's refined copper market, but pulled out last year after the scandal broke, said Atikhom Thongnamtako, senior executive vice president at major buyer Bangkok Cable Co.

"The firm stopped supplying since late last year. It had a lot of in-house clearing to do. Codelco of Chile is now taking over as a major supplier of copper cathode in Thailand, followed by Mitsui and Mitsubishi who distribute copper mostly from Zambia," he said.
Thailand's demand for copper cathode in 1996 was estimated by traders at between 150,000-170,000 tonnes and is growing by about 10 percent a year.
Sumitomo appears to have largely held onto its copper market share in Malaysia, local industry sources said.
"They've curtailed their operations in many countries but they're still doing some routine supplies here," an official at a copper cable company in Kuala Lumpur said.
Industry executives said the Malaysian market had not really been affected by the Sumitomo incident as about 56 percent of its supplies of refined copper came from Chile, Australia and Zambia.
Sumitomo only provided about 10 to 15 percent of the copper cathode needed by Malaysian industries, one source said.
In Indonesia, it has also been business as usual with no staff retrenchments or loss of business in the year since the Hamanaka debacle, a local Sumitomo Corp official said.

"Things have been normal and nothing has changed," he told Reuters. "We are doing business as usual. Staffings levels have been about the same although some local employees have resigned...but not because of the tragedy."
